question: A cardiology analytics client is comparing two ways to use language models on ECGs: report generation with retrieved criteria (RAG-TRACE) and direct diagnostic option scoring (ECGJev). How does ECGJev work and perform, what evidence shows it relies on the ECG signal, what does RAG-TRACE show about retrieved criteria as evidence, and is either validated for clinical use?

evidence.text: Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evaluated using Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment using Uni-G and comparison against expert-validated diagnostic labels. Results: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. A deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications, including 639 without numeric checks, while preserving 268 of 269 applications independently supported by Uni-G. Restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%. Under matched instructions and an identical output schema, retrieval increased unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained unchanged at 62.6%. Conclusion: These findings identify a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation: retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence. Measurement-based verification can reduce unsupported criterion applications, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evaluated using Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment using Uni-G and comparison against expert-validated diagnostic labels. Results: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. A deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications, including 639 without numeric checks, while preserving 268 of 269 applications independently supported by Uni-G. Restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%. Under matched instructions and an identical output schema, retrieval increased unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained unchanged at 62.6%. Conclusion: These findings identify a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation: retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence. Measurement-based verification can reduce unsupported criterion applications, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

evidence.text: . These advances highlight the importance of evidence quality, but the reliability of retrieved criteria in ECG report generation remains insufficiently examined. ECG interpretation depends on standardized criteria, including QRS duration, Sokolow–Lyon voltage, and corrected QT intervals Surawicz et al. (2009) ; Sokolow and Lyon (1949) ; Hancock et al. (2009) ; Casale et al. (1985) ; Peguero et al. (2017) ; Bazett (1920) ; Rautaharju et al. (2009) ; Prineas et al. (2010) . Clinical guidelines establish measurable thresholds and diagnostic definitions Mason et al. (2007) ; Wagner et al. (2009) ; Thygesen et al. (2018) . A retrieved criterion may be clinically relevant without being satisfied by the patient’s measurements. Other retrieved information, such as calibration settings or laboratory values, may lack a corresponding ECG measurement. These limitations create a critical gap between retrieval relevance and verifiable diagnostic evidence. This study presents RAG-TRACE, a measurement-based framework for evaluating retrieved criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. We analyze 1,083 held-out PTB-XL patients using 47 criteria cards, including 14 with numeric checks and 33 without measurable verification rules. Structured reports are generated with and without retrieval. A deterministic rule evaluates applied criteria against Marquette 12SL measurements, while Uni-G provides independent assessment. Diagnostic agreement and completeness are evaluated separately against expert-validated labels. Additional experiments assess retrieval constraints, controlled generation settings, and generalizability to other physiological recordings

evidence.text: The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is an essential diagnostic tool for assessing cardiac activity through measurable intervals, axes, and voltages Kligfield et al. (2007) ; Mason et al. (2007) . Large datasets such as PTB-XL, comprising 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients Wagner et al. (2020) , have advanced automated ECG interpretation Strodthoff et al. (2021) . Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in detecting cardiac abnormalities Ribeiro et al. (2020) ; Hannun et al. (2019) ; Alday et al. (2020) ; Mehari and Strodthoff (2022) and supporting cardiovascular screening Attia et al. (2019) ; Siontis et al. (2021) . Nevertheless, generating reliable clinical reports requires more than diagnostic predictions. Each reported finding must be supported by patient-specific evidence. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential for generating clinical narratives Tu et al. (2025) and diagnostic explanations Singhal et al. (2023) ; Nori et al. (2023) . Their outputs can contain unsupported statements and inaccurate evidence attribution Ji et al. (2023) ; Maynez et al. (2020) . Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates external knowledge to improve factual grounding Lewis et al. (2020) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Shuster et al. (2021) , with promising applications in medical question answering Xiong et al. (2024) ; Zakka et al. (2024) and clinical information extraction Agrawal et al. (2022) . Recent studies have investigated evidence alignment in clinical question answering Irankhah and Fodeh (2026) and query-level reliability in retriever upgrades Irankhah and Arif (2026) . These advances highlight the importance of evidence quality, but the reliability of retrieved criteria in ECG report generation remains insufficiently examined

evidence.text: RAG-TRACE establishes a measurement-centered approach to assessing evidence reliability in AI-generated ECG reports. The evaluation highlights the importance of distinguishing retrieved clinical information from criteria supported by patient-specific measurements. Its verification mechanism provides a transparent means of identifying unsupported applications while preserving valid quantitative evidence. Importantly, criterion-level reliability and diagnostic completeness represent separate dimensions of report quality that require independent assessment. Integrating these principles into clinical RAG pipelines could support more interpretable and auditable AI-generated reports. Future work should extend RAG-TRACE to broader clinical datasets, incorporate measurement-aware retrieval, and evaluate its impact through clinician-adjudicated assessments.

evidence.text: Retrieval-augmented ECG reporting exposes a gap between clinical relevance and patient-specific evidence. Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1 mini reports, with 639 of 647 withdrawn applications lacking numeric checks. Qwen3-8B exhibited a distinct failure pattern, with 203 of 211 measurement-disconfirmed applications independently rejected by Uni-G. The differences highlight two sources of unreliable reporting: unverifiable retrieved content and incorrect application of measurable criteria. The deliberately constructed criteria library increased exposure to these failures, limiting generalization to routine clinical practice. RAG-TRACE complements research on retrieval robustness, medical citation reliability, and multi-step clinical reasoning Park and Lee (2024) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Wind et al. (2025) by assessing retrieved evidence against patient-specific measurements. Verification preserved 268 of 269 independently supported GPT-4.1 mini applications and 274 of 282 Qwen3-8B applications. This selective withdrawal offers that unsupported criteria can be removed with limited loss of measurement-supported claims. The zero release score reflects the deterministic rule itself, making independent measurement agreement essential for assessing verification performance. Controlled comparisons further distinguish retrieval effects from changes in diagnostic scoring. Under identical instructions and output schemas, unsupported-criterion reports increased from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained at 62.6%. The different-schema comparison showed a modest decrease in micro-F1 (0.804 to 0.795) and scored hypertrophy recall (0.617 to 0.514)

evidence.text: The evaluation relied on published PTB-XL diagnostic labels without independent clinical review of generated reports. The prespecified affirmation rule undercounted diagnostic assertions, while the exploratory label-aware analysis excluded 138 sentences with disagreement between judges. Model comparisons were constrained by incomplete JSON generation for Llama, 112 paired DeepSeek cases, and the use of a single closed model for numeric-only retrieval. The identical-schema and different-schema comparisons addressed distinct experimental conditions. BM25 was evaluated without report generation, and TF–IDF did not incorporate biomedical embeddings. The reported cue-list contrast was significant ( p=0.008 ); the other comparisons were exploratory. The absence of prospective clinical evaluation limits conclusions about diagnostic safety and real-world applicability.

evidence.text: . Affirmed diagnoses were extracted using the prespecified cue-based rule and, separately, the exploratory label-aware approach. Since verification modifies only criterion applications, diagnostic consistency remains unchanged after withdrawal. An additional statement-level metric assessed discrepancies between the original eight criteria and their linked cardiologist statement codes, including unsupported applications and omitted findings. Diagnostic agreement was quantified using micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 across the five superclasses. Class-specific recall was calculated among patients with the corresponding reference diagnosis, while patient-level recall measured the proportion of reference superclasses identified in each report. Paired effects were expressed as \Delta=\theta_{\mathrm{key}}-\theta_{\mathrm{none}} , comparing keyword retrieval with no retrieval on the same patients. Confidence intervals were obtained from 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

evidence.text: . The different-schema comparison showed a modest decrease in micro-F1 (0.804 to 0.795) and scored hypertrophy recall (0.617 to 0.514). Six of the 11 apparent hypertrophy losses involved hypertension statements assigned hypertrophy labels. Such discrepancies illustrate how output structure and scoring definitions can influence apparent diagnostic performance. For clinical RAG systems, evidence retrieval and criterion verification serve distinct purposes. A clinically relevant criterion requires measurable patient support before its application can be justified. Deterministic verification can address unsupported criterion claims without modifying diagnostic statements. Measurement agreement, diagnostic completeness, and clinical validity must therefore be assessed independently.

evidence.text: A separate different-schema comparison used the same instructions but allowed criterion claims only when retrieved cards were present. Micro-F1 decreased from 0.804 to 0.795 (difference -0.009 , 95% CI -0.014 to -0.004 ), while scored hypertrophy recall decreased from 0.617 to 0.514 (Table 8 ). The expert-absent diagnosis rate changed from 17.5% to 16.7% ( p=0.077 ). Of 11 scored hypertrophy losses, six no-card credits involved a stored HYP label attached to hypertension wording. Other discrepancies involved denied voltage criteria, qualified diagnoses, or endorsements outside diagnosis claims. These scores do not represent 11 clinically missed diagnoses. The identical-schema comparison showed unchanged hypertrophy recall. An earlier identifier-constrained comparison joined against a different no-card prompt showed a larger recall decline (0.772 to 0.546), which cannot be attributed solely to retrieval. evidence.text: The prespecified cue list recognized only 3 of 15 audited ordinary diagnosis sentences and omitted 846 of 1,360 keyword-note diagnosis sentences. An exploratory label-aware rule was therefore evaluated separately. In a 1,000-sentence audit, two language-model judges agreed on 862 sentences. Against their shared labels, the label-aware rule achieved micro-F1 of 0.932, compared with 0.435 for the cue list. Under the label-aware rule, GPT-4.1 mini expert-absent diagnosis rates increased from 19.8% without cards to 23.0% with keyword cards (95% CI for the difference: 0.016–0.049). In the matched-prompt comparison, rates were 21.2% and 22.1%, with a confidence interval including zero. Effects differed across models: Qwen3-14B and MedGemma 4B showed lower expert-absent rates with retrieval, Gemma 3 12B showed a higher rate, and Qwen3-8B showed little change (Table 7 ). Figures 4 , 5 , and 6 summarize class recall, diagnostic precision, micro-F1, and expert-absent diagnosis rates across the saved original-prompt comparisons. Exploratory label-aware expert-absent rates. A counted diagnosis is a saved superclass label that the sentence does not negate. The no-card column for the numeric-only and constrained arms is the original no-card note, joined by electrocardiogram identifier. Intervals are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Diagnosis agreement for the same models. A, class recall with no retrieval. B, class recall with keyword retrieval. C, notes with a false diagnosis. D, micro-F1. In C and D, blue is no retrieval and green is keyword retrieval. Sample sizes are 1,083 except Qwen3-8B (1,082), MedGemma (850), and DeepSeek (112). DeepSeek is a selected subset. Precision, recall, micro-F1, and false-diagnosis notes for the six models with a full paired sample

evidence.text: For the eight criteria linked to cardiologist statement codes, keyword retrieval increased statement mismatch from 7.5% to 24.9% for GPT-4.1 mini and from 1.6% to 34.1% for Qwen3-8B. The two-algorithm agreement rule reduced these rates to 22.2% and 19.6%, respectively, without a substantial increase in unstated linked findings (Table 5 ). Among retained applications, the linked code was present in 27.5% of 204 GPT-4.1 mini applications and 12.8% of 218 Qwen3-8B applications. Numeric support and diagnostic-label agreement therefore remained distinct. Statement mismatch against stored cardiologist codes for the original eight checks, and the mean number of those findings left unstated.

searches.query: A cardiology analytics client is comparing two ways to use language models on ECGs: report generation with retrieved criteria (RAG-TRACE) and direct diagnostic option scoring (ECGJev). How does ECGJev work and perform, what evidence shows it relies on the ECG signal, what does RAG-TRACE show about retrieved criteria as evidence, and is either validated for clinical use?
